Assume $\widehat A_c$ is certified Hurwitz, $\mathcal L$ is invertible on Hermitian matrices, and outward-verified bounds satisfy
$$\kappa\ge\|\mathcal L^{-1}\|_{F\to F},\quad r\ge\|F_c(\widehat X)\|_F,\quad g\ge\|G\|_2,$$
with $\rho>0$ such that
$$\kappa(r+g\rho^2)\le\rho,\qquad 2\kappa g\rho<1.$$
Then there is exactly one Hermitian CARE root in the closed Frobenius ball $\|X-\widehat X\|_F\le\rho$.

If also a verified Hermitian $W\succ0$ and $\gamma>0$ satisfy
$$-(\widehat A_c^*W+W\widehat A_c)\succeq\gamma I,\qquad 2\|W\|_2g\rho<\gamma,$$
then that root is Hurwitz-stabilizing. Under the standard CARE hypotheses of [[thm-care-stabilizing-psd-solution-and-value]], it is the unique stabilizing positive-semidefinite solution.

Let $\widehat X=\widehat X^*$ be a DARE candidate, $S(X)=R+B^*XB$, $K(X)=S(X)^{-1}B^*XA$, $A_c(X)=A-BK(X)$, and let
$$F_d(X)=Q+A^*XA-A^*XB S(X)^{-1}B^*XA-X.$$
Suppose $S(\widehat X)\succeq\delta_0I$ is outward-certified. For a proposed radius $\rho>0$ put
$$a=\|A\|_2,\quad b=\|B\|_2,\quad m=\|\widehat X\|_F+\rho,\quad \delta=\delta_0-b^2\rho.$$
Require $\delta>0$ and define
$$L_K=\frac{ab}{\delta}+\frac{ab^3m}{\delta^2},\quad M_c=a+\frac{ab^2m}{\delta},\quad L_c=bL_K,\quad L_D=2M_cL_c.$$
Let $D(E)=A_c(\widehat X)^*EA_c(\widehat X)-E$ be invertible on Hermitian matrices, with outward-certified $\kappa\ge\|D^{-1}\|_{F\to F}$ and $r\ge\|F_d(\widehat X)\|_F$. If
$$\kappa(r+L_D\rho^2/2)\le\rho,\qquad \kappa L_D\rho<1,$$
there is exactly one Hermitian DARE root in the closed Frobenius $\rho$-ball, and $R+B^*XB\succeq\delta I$ throughout that ball.

For the stabilizing branch, additionally suppose $\widehat A_c=A_c(\widehat X)$ is Schur stable and an outward-certified $W\succ0$ satisfies
$$W-\widehat A_c^*W\widehat A_c\succeq\gamma I.$$
If, with $\eta=L_c\rho$,
$$\|W\|_2(2M_c\eta+\eta^2)<\gamma,$$
then the root is Schur-stabilizing. Under the standard DARE hypotheses of [[thm-dare-stabilizing-psd-solution-and-value]], it is the unique stabilizing positive-semidefinite solution.

Let $F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, $m,n\ge1$, $A\in F^{m\times m}$ and $B\in F^{n\times n}$. Spectra of real matrices are taken over $\mathbb C$. The map $\mathcal S_{A,B}$ of [[def-sylvester-operator-and-separation-number]] is invertible if and only if

$$
\sigma(A)\cap(-\sigma(B))=\varnothing.
$$

Equivalently, for every $C\in F^{m\times n}$, the equation $AX+XB=C$ has a unique solution if and only if this spectral condition holds. The same condition is equivalent to $\operatorname{sep}(A,-B)>0$.

Let $X$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and assume
$X$ admits an ordered basis of finite length. Then $X$ is a Banach space in the
sense of [[def-banach-space]].

Let $M\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ be Schur stable and let $r$ satisfy $\rho(M)<r<1$. For the Euclidean induced operator norm there is a finite $C_r$ such that
$$\|M^k\|_2\le C_r r^k\qquad(k\ge0).$$
For a real matrix, interpret the same statement on its complexification.

For compatible linear maps between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces,

$$\lVert ST\rVert\le \lVert S\rVert\,\lVert T\rVert.$$

For every such linear map $T$,

$$\lVert T^*T\rVert=\lVert T\rVert^2.$$

Let $A\in F^{n\times n}$ be Hurwitz and let $Q=Q^*\in F^{n\times n}$. Then the improper matrix integral

$$
X=\int_0^\infty e^{tA}Qe^{tA^*}\,dt
$$

converges and is the unique solution of $AX+XA^*+Q=0$. If $Q\succeq0$, then $X\succeq0$. If $Q\succ0$, then $X\succ0$. For $Q\succeq0$, $X\succ0$ if and only if there is no nonzero $v$ for which $e^{tA^*}v\in\ker Q^{1/2}$ for every $t\ge0$.

Let $(N,M)$ be the order-$2n$ DARE pencil in [[prop-dare-symplectic-pencil-graph-and-stable-spectrum]], with $n\ge1$. Work over $\mathbb C$, also for real input. Suppose exact unitary matrices $Q,V$ give an ordered complex generalized Schur pair
$$Q^*NV=S=\begin{bmatrix}S_{11}&S_{12}\\0&S_{22}\end{bmatrix},\qquad Q^*MV=T=\begin{bmatrix}T_{11}&T_{12}\\0&T_{22}\end{bmatrix},$$
where each diagonal block has order $n$, all four diagonal blocks are upper triangular, the leading homogeneous roots are strictly inside the unit disk, and the trailing roots are strictly outside its closure, including infinity. This ordered representation is an explicit input; existence of an unordered generalized Schur form is not an ordering certificate.

Give pairs of $n\times n$ matrices the product Frobenius norm
$$\|(Y,Z)\|_P=(\|Y\|_F^2+\|Z\|_F^2)^{1/2},$$
and define the lower-oriented generalized Sylvester separation
$$\gamma=\min_{\|(Y,Z)\|_P=1}\|(S_{22}Y-ZS_{11},T_{22}Y-ZT_{11})\|_P.$$
Then $\gamma>0$. Write $\kappa=\gamma^{-1}$, $h=(\|S_{12}\|_2^2+\|T_{12}\|_2^2)^{1/2}$. For arbitrary pencil perturbations $\Delta_N,\Delta_M$, put $E=Q^*\Delta_NV$, $F=Q^*\Delta_MV$, and $\delta=(\|E\|_F^2+\|F\|_F^2)^{1/2}=(\|\Delta_N\|_F^2+\|\Delta_M\|_F^2)^{1/2}$. If $r>0$ satisfies
$$\kappa[\delta+2\delta r+(h+\delta)r^2]\le r,\qquad \kappa[2\delta+2(h+\delta)r]<1,$$
there is a unique pair $(Y,Z)$ in the product radius-$r$ ball for which the right and left graphs $V[I;Y]$ and $Q[I;Z]$ form matching deflating spaces of the perturbed pair. In particular $\|Y\|_F,\|Z\|_F\le r$. For $\delta>0$, a sufficient choice is $r=2\kappa\delta$ whenever, with $\theta=\kappa\delta$,
$$4\theta+4\kappa h\theta+4\theta^2<1.$$
For $\delta=0$, take $Y=Z=0$.

Here are separate sufficient margins identifying these graphs as the stable spaces. Set
$$a=\delta+(\|S_{12}\|_2+\delta)r,\qquad b=\delta+(\|T_{12}\|_2+\delta)r,$$
$$K_s=T_{11}^{-1}S_{11},\qquad K_u=S_{22}^{-1}T_{22}.$$
The inverses exist and $K_s,K_u$ are Schur stable. For $j=s,u$, choose $W_j\succ0$ with $W_j-K_j^*W_jK_j=I$; the convergent Stein series supplies such a matrix. Require
$$\|T_{11}^{-1}\|_2b<1,\qquad \|S_{22}^{-1}\|_2a<1,$$
and define
$$\epsilon_s=\frac{\|T_{11}^{-1}\|_2(a+b\|K_s\|_2)}{1-\|T_{11}^{-1}\|_2b},\qquad \epsilon_u=\frac{\|S_{22}^{-1}\|_2(b+a\|K_u\|_2)}{1-\|S_{22}^{-1}\|_2a}.$$
If
$$\|W_j\|_2(2\|K_j\|_2\epsilon_j+\epsilon_j^2)<1\qquad(j=s,u),$$
then the perturbed pencil is regular, has precisely $n$ stable roots and $n$ outside roots, and the constructed right graph is its stable deflating space. For fixed ordered input these margins hold for all sufficiently small $\delta$ with $r=2\kappa\delta$.

For normalized right bases, write $V=[U\ V_2]$ and
$$\widehat U=(U+V_2Y)(I+Y^*Y)^{-1/2},\qquad y=\|Y\|_2,\qquad \beta(y)=\sqrt{2\left(1-\frac1{\sqrt{1+y^2}}\right)}.$$
Then $\widehat U^*\widehat U=I$, $\|\widehat U-U\|_2=\beta(y)\le y\le r$, and
$$\|(I-UU^*)\widehat U\|_2=\frac{y}{\sqrt{1+y^2}}.$$
If the physical top block $U_1$ of $U=[U_1;U_2]$ is invertible, $X=U_2U_1^{-1}$, and $\|U_1^{-1}\|_2\beta(y)<1$, then $\widehat U_1$ is invertible and
$$\|\widehat U_2\widehat U_1^{-1}-X\|_2\le\frac{(1+\|X\|_2)\beta(y)}{\|U_1^{-1}\|_2^{-1}-\beta(y)}.$$
For the directly computable bound with $\beta(r)$, impose the stronger margin $\|U_1^{-1}\|_2\beta(r)<1$; replacing $\beta(y)$ by $\beta(r)$ then gives a valid weaker estimate. An independently rotated orthonormal basis of the same perturbed space produces the identical chart, so it need not be close to $U$ before alignment. The conclusion concerns an unstructured perturbed pencil; it does not certify Hermitian symmetry, Riccati residual, positive data, or the stabilizing Riccati branch after symmetrization.

derivations.claim: By [F3], expanding the CARE polynomial at a Hermitian $X$ gives $F_c(X+E)-F_c(X)=\mathcal L_c^X(E)-EGE,$ where $\mathcal L_c^X(E)=(A-GX)^*E+E(A-GX)$. For the DARE, set $f(X)=Q+A^*X(I+GX)^{-1}A$. Direct multiplication gives $\Phi_G(X+E)-\Phi_G(X)=(I+(X+E)G)^{-1}E(I+GX)^{-1},\quad \Phi_G(X)=X(I+GX)^{-1}.$ Taking the derivative at $E=0$ and multiplying by $A^*,A$ gives $Df(X)[E]=A_c(X)^*EA_c(X)$; since $F_d=f-X$, this gives $DF_d(X)[E]=A_c(X)^*EA_c(X)-E$.

Apply [F14] to the exact ordered unitary DARE pencil representation and the supplied perturbations of both pencil matrices. Its paired generalized Sylvester operator and contraction inequalities give the radius-$r$ right and left deflating graphs; its separate Neumann and Stein margins establish the perturbed stable split. Its normalized basis construction gives distance at most $\beta(r)\le r$, and its computable physical chart estimate retains the inverse graph-block norm and the strict margin $\|U_1^{-1}\|_2\beta(r)<1$. No part of this conclusion follows from QZ backward error alone.

For a CARE additive residual perturbation $\Delta$, write $X=X_c+E$ and let $\delta=\|\Delta\|_F$. Then $F_c(X_c)=0$ and step 1.1 makes the perturbed root equation equivalent to $E=-\mathcal L_c^{-1}\Delta+\mathcal L_c^{-1}(EGE).$ If $\rho$ satisfies $\kappa_c(\delta+\|G\|_2\rho^2)\le\rho$ and $2\kappa_c\|G\|_2\rho<1$, the map sends the closed radius-$\rho$ Hermitian ball to itself and has Lipschitz constant at most the second displayed quantity. Iteration from zero gives geometric successive differences; [F10] gives a limit in the ball, continuity gives a fixed point, and contraction gives uniqueness. Let $W_c=\int_0^\infty e^{tA_c^*}e^{tA_c}\,dt\succ0$; then $A_c^*W_c+W_cA_c=-I$. If also $2\|W_c\|_2\|G\|_2\rho<1$, then $\|EGW_c+W_cGE\|_2\le2\|W_c\|_2\|G\|_2\rho<1$. Hence $(A_c-GE)^*W_c+W_c(A_c-GE)\prec0$; an eigenvector $v$ with eigenvalue $\lambda$ gives $2\operatorname{Re}(\lambda)v^*W_cv<0$, so the perturbed loop is Hurwitz. For DARE, [F2] gives Schur stability and [F11] gives the Stein inverse $\mathcal L_d^{-1}(Y)=-\sum_{k\ge0}(A_c^*)^kYA_c^k$. On a sufficiently small ball, $S(X)=R+B^*XB\succeq\delta_S I$, where $\delta_S=\lambda_{\min}S(X_d)-b^2\rho>0$. Put $a=\|A\|_2$, $b=\|B\|_2$, and $m=\|X_d\|_F+\rho$. The resolvent identity gives $\|S(X)^{-1}\|_2\le\delta_S^{-1}$ and $\|S(X)^{-1}-S(Y)^{-1}\|_2\le b^2\delta_S^{-2}\|X-Y\|_F$. Splitting $K(X)-K(Y)$ into its $X$ and inverse-factor changes yields $\|K(X)-K(Y)\|_F\le L_K\|X-Y\|_F$, where $L_K=ab/\delta_S+ab^3m/\delta_S^2$; hence $\|A_c(X)\|_2\le M_c=a+ab^2m/\delta_S$ and $\|A_c(X)-A_c(Y)\|_2\le L_c\|X-Y\|_F$, $L_c=bL_K$. Since $DF_d(X)[E]=A_c(X)^*EA_c(X)-E$, subtraction gives $\|DF_d(X)-DF_d(Y)\|_{F\to F}\le2M_cL_c\|X-Y\|_F=:L_D\|X-Y\|_F$. Integrating this derivative along line segments gives $R(E)=F_d(X_d+E)-F_d(X_d)-\mathcal L_d(E)$ with $\|R(E)\|_F\le L_D\|E\|_F^2/2$ and $\|R(E)-R(F)\|_F\le L_D\rho\|E-F\|_F$ on the ball. Thus $E=-\mathcal L_d^{-1}(\Delta+R(E))$ is a self-map when $\kappa_d(\delta+L_D\rho^2/2)\le\rho$ and a contraction when $\kappa_d L_D\rho<1$. The same completeness argument gives its unique local root. For a separate stability margin, take $W_d=\sum_{k\ge0}(A_c^*)^kA_c^k\succ0$, so $W_d-A_c^*W_dA_c=I$ by [F11]. Put $\eta=L_c\rho$. Expanding the Stein form bounds its change by $\|W_d\|_2(2M_c\eta+\eta^2)$; choose $\rho$ so this is below $1$. Then $W_d-A_c(X)^*W_dA_c(X)\succ0$, and an eigenvector gives $(1-|\lambda|^2)v^*W_dv>0$, so the perturbed loop is Schur stable. For sufficiently small $\delta>0$, take $\rho=2\kappa_c\delta$ in CARE when $\|G\|_2>0$; the contraction and stability inequalities hold for small enough $\delta$, giving $\|E\|_F=O(\delta)$. If $G=0$, the equation is linear and this order bound is exact. In DARE, take $\rho=2\kappa_d\delta$ when $L_D>0$; for sufficiently small $\delta$ this satisfies the self-map, contraction, $S(X)\succ0$, and Stein-margin bounds, again giving $\|E\|_F=O(\delta)$. If $L_D=0$, the local equation is linear. The remainders are therefore $O(\delta^2)$, proving the first-order terms $-\mathcal L_c^{-1}\Delta$ and $-\mathcal L_d^{-1}\Delta$.

Put $T_X=[I\ 0;X_c\ I]$. Multiplying the Hamiltonian in [F4] on the right by $T_X$ and then on the left by $T_X^{-1}=[I\ 0;-X_c\ I]$, and using the CARE identity in [F3], gives $T_X^{-1}HT_X=\begin{bmatrix}A_c&-G\\0&-A_c^*\end{bmatrix}.$ The Sylvester map $\mathcal S(Y)=-A_c^*Y-YA_c$ has smallest singular value $\sigma=\operatorname{sep}(-A_c^*,A_c)>0$: [F9] applies because $\sigma(-A_c^*)$ lies in the right half-plane while $-\sigma(-A_c)=\sigma(A_c)$ lies in the left half-plane; [F6] gives inverse norm $\kappa_s=1/\sigma$. In the perturbed coordinates, write $Z=[Z_{ij}]$ and seek an invariant graph $[I;Y]$. Its lower-block graph equation is $-A_c^*Y-YA_c+Z_{21}+Z_{22}Y-YZ_{11}+YGY-YZ_{12}Y=0.$ Hence $Y$ is a fixed point of $\mathcal T(Y)=-\mathcal S^{-1}(Z_{21}+Z_{22}Y-YZ_{11}+YGY-YZ_{12}Y).$ On the Frobenius ball $\|Y\|_F\le2\theta$, each block norm of $Z$ is at most $\zeta$. The map norm is at most $\kappa_s[\zeta+2\zeta\|Y\|_F+(\|G\|_2+\zeta)\|Y\|_F^2]$, hence at most $\theta+4\theta^2+4\mu\theta^2+4\theta^3\le2\theta$ under the displayed smallness condition. Its Lipschitz constant is at most $2\theta+4\mu\theta+4\theta^2<1$. Completeness [F10] and iteration therefore give a unique fixed point in the ball. Returning through $T_X$ turns $[I;Y]$ into $[I;X_c+Y]$, proving the graph bound. Under [A2], the restriction has $n$ stable eigenvalues and the perturbed matrix has exactly $n$ stable eigenvalues in total. In a basis beginning with this invariant graph, the perturbed matrix is block upper triangular with this stable restriction as its first diagonal block; the quotient block therefore has no stable eigenvalues. A stable generalized eigenvector must project to a stable generalized eigenvector of the quotient, which is impossible, so every stable generalized eigenspace lies in the graph. Both spaces have dimension $n$, hence the graph is the stable spectral subspace.

Since $\widetilde U_1=U_1+\Delta U_1=U_1(I+U_1^{-1}\Delta U_1)$ and $\|U_1^{-1}\Delta U_1\|_2<1$, the Neumann geometric series makes the second factor invertible and gives $\|\widetilde U_1^{-1}\|_2\le(\|U_1^{-1}\|_2^{-1}-\|\Delta U_1\|_2)^{-1}$. Using $U_2=XU_1$, $\widetilde U_2\widetilde U_1^{-1}-X=(\Delta U_2-X\Delta U_1)\widetilde U_1^{-1}.$ Submultiplicativity [F12] proves the displayed basis-chart bound. This derivation uses only the graph equation, so it applies to both the CARE invariant graph and the DARE deflating graph; it does not convert a pencil backward error into a deflating-subspace error.

citations.quote:
Let $A\in F^{n\times n}$, $B\in F^{n\times m}$, $C\in F^{p\times n}$, $R=R^*\succ0$, and $Q=C^*C$. Assume $(A,B)$ is discretely stabilizable and $(A,C)$ discretely detectable, using [[def-lqr-stabilizability-and-detectability]]. Then the DARE of [[def-standard-continuous-and-discrete-riccati-equations]] has exactly one Hermitian positive-semidefinite solution $X$. For the equivalent Riccati map $f(P)=Q+A^*P(I+GP)^{-1}A$, its finite-horizon iterates $P_0=0$, $P_{k+1}=f(P_k)$ satisfy $0\preceq P_k\uparrow X$. For all Hermitian positive-semidefinite $Y,Z$,
$$f(Y)-f(Z)=A_c(Y)^*(Y-Z)A_c(Z),\qquad A_c(Y)=(I+GY)^{-1}A.$$
The solution satisfies $R+B^*XB\succ0$, and its closed loop $A_c=A-B(R+B^*XB)^{-1}B^*XA$ is Schur stable. For each $x_0$, the infinite-horizon discrete cost
$$\inf_{(u_k)}\sum_{k=0}^\infty(x_k^*Qx_k+u_k^*Ru_k),\qquad x_{k+1}=Ax_k+Bu_k,$$
over sequences with finite cost equals $x_0^*Xx_0$ and is attained by $u_k=-K_dx_k$. Singular $A$ is allowed throughout; no inverse of $A$ is used.

For Hermitian $G,H\succeq0$, define $\Phi_G(X)=X(I+GX)^{-1}$ and $f(X)=H+A^*\Phi_G(X)A$ on $X\succeq0$. One doubling step in [[alg-finite-budget-structure-preserving-doubling-for-dare]] is well-defined, preserves $G_j,H_j\succeq0$, and its updated triple satisfies
$$f\circ f(X)=H_1+A_1^*X(I+G_1X)^{-1}A_1,$$
where
$$A_1=A(I+GH)^{-1}A,\quad G_1=G+A(I+GH)^{-1}GA^*,\quad H_1=H+A^*H(I+GH)^{-1}A.$$
Consequently, if $f_0=f$ and the recurrence is iterated, then $H_j=f^{2^j}(0)$.

Let $M\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ be Schur stable and let $r$ satisfy $\rho(M)<r<1$. For the Euclidean induced operator norm there is a finite $C_r$ such that
$$\|M^k\|_2\le C_r r^k\qquad(k\ge0).$$
For a real matrix, interpret the same statement on its complexification.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be non-negative. Then there exists a unique non-negative operator
$R:V\to V$ such that

$$R^2=T.$$

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, and
let $\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$ be the positive singular values of
$A$, where $r=\operatorname{rank}A$; write $\sigma_1=0$ when $r=0$.

1. **Spectral formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_2=\sigma_1$, where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is
   the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].
2. **Frobenius formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_F=\bigl(\sigma_1^{2}+\cdots+\sigma_r^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}$.
3. **Unitary invariance.** For every unitary $U\in M_m(\mathbb F)$ and
   $V\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ (over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$: orthogonal matrices),
   $$\lVert UAV\rVert_2=\lVert A\rVert_2,\qquad \lVert UAV\rVert_F=\lVert A\rVert_F.$$
4. **Sharp rank comparison.**
   $$\lVert A\rVert_2\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_F\;\le\;\sqrt{r}\,\lVert A\rVert_2.$$
   The lower inequality is an equality exactly when $r\le 1$; the upper
   inequality is an equality exactly when $\sigma_1=\cdots=\sigma_r$, that is,
   when all nonzero singular values coincide. In particular
   $\lVert A\rVert_F\le\sqrt{\min(m,n)}\,\lVert A\rVert_2$.

derivations.claim: By [F2], $H_j=P_{2^j}$ and $G_j,H_j$ remain positive semidefinite. Since [F1] gives $P_k\to X_*$, the subsequence $H_j=P_{2^j}$ also converges to $X_*$. No inverse of $A$ is used.

Put $M=A_c(X_*)$. By [F1], $M$ is Schur stable; [F3] therefore makes $W=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(M^*)^kM^k$ converge in norm. It is positive definite, $W\succeq I$, and $M^*WM=W-I$. If $w=\|W\|_2$, then $v^*M^*WMv\le(1-w^{-1})v^*Wv$, so the induced $W$-norm $\|M\|_W:=\|W^{1/2}MW^{-1/2}\|_2$ is at most $q_0=\sqrt{1-w^{-1}}<1$. Choose $q$ with $q_0<q<1$. Since $P_k\to X_*$ and $A_c(P_k)$ is continuous on $P_k\succeq0$, choose $k_0$ so $\|A_c(P_k)\|_W\le q$ for all $k\ge k_0$.

Let $E_k=X_*-P_k\succeq0$. The Riccati-map difference identity in [F1] gives $E_{k+1}=M^*E_kA_c(P_k).$ Define $\|E\|_{F,W^{-1}}=\|W^{-1/2}EW^{-1/2}\|_F$. By [F5], for $k\ge k_0$, $\|E_{k+1}\|_{F,W^{-1}}\le\|M\|_W\|A_c(P_k)\|_W\|E_k\|_{F,W^{-1}}\le q^2\|E_k\|_{F,W^{-1}}.$ Iteration gives $\|E_k\|_{F,W^{-1}}\le\|E_{k_0}\|_{F,W^{-1}}q^{2(k-k_0)}$. Taking $k=2^j$ and setting $C=\max\{1,\|E_{k_0}\|_{F,W^{-1}}q^{-2k_0}\}$ proves the displayed envelope for all $2^j\ge k_0$. Since $C>0$, direct calculation gives $\epsilon_{j+1}=Cq^{2^{j+2}}=\epsilon_j^2/C$.

citations.quote:
Let $F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, $A\in F^{n\times n}$, $B\in F^{n\times m}$, $C\in F^{p\times n}$, and $R=R^*\in F^{m\times m}$ be positive definite. Write $Q=C^*C$ and $G=BR^{-1}B^*$. The inverse $R^{-1}$ is well-defined: [[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]] supplies an invertible factor $R=LL^*$, so $R^{-1}=L^{-*}L^{-1}$. Thus $v^*Gv=\|L^{-1}B^*v\|_2^2\ge0$ and $v^*Qv=\|Cv\|_2^2\ge0$. The symbol $^*$ is transpose over $\mathbb R$ and conjugate transpose over $\mathbb C$.

The **continuous algebraic Riccati equation (CARE)** is
$$A^*X+XA-XGX+Q=0.$$
Its residual is $F_c(X)=A^*X+XA-XGX+Q$, its feedback is $K_c(X)=R^{-1}B^*X$, and its closed-loop matrix is $A_c(X)=A-BK_c(X)=A-GX$.

For $X=X^*\succeq0$, $S_X:=R+B^*XB$ is positive definite because
$v^*S_Xv=v^*Rv+(Bv)^*X(Bv)>0$ for every nonzero $v$. The **discrete
algebraic Riccati equation (DARE)** is
$$X=Q+A^*XA-A^*XB(R+B^*XB)^{-1}B^*XA.$$
Its residual is $F_d(X)=Q+A^*XA-A^*XB(R+B^*XB)^{-1}B^*XA-X$. Whenever $X=X^*$, the matrix $R+B^*XB$ is positive definite if $X\succeq0$. Its feedback and closed-loop matrix are
$$K_d(X)=(R+B^*XB)^{-1}B^*XA,\qquad A_c(X)=A-BK_d(X).$$
A CARE solution is **stabilizing** when it is Hermitian and $A_c(X)$ is Hurwitz. A DARE solution is **stabilizing** when it is Hermitian, $R+B^*XB\succ0$, and $A_c(X)$ is Schur stable. No inverse of $A$ is part of either definition.

For Hermitian $X$ with $S_X$ invertible, multiplication gives
$$(I+GX)^{-1}=I-BS_X^{-1}B^*X,\qquad X(I+GX)^{-1}=X-XB S_X^{-1}B^*X.$$
In either product, the additional coefficient of $B$ is
$R^{-1}-S_X^{-1}-S_X^{-1}(B^*XB)R^{-1}=0$, because
$S_X=R+B^*XB$. Thus the DARE is equivalently
$X=Q+A^*X(I+GX)^{-1}A$, and its closed-loop matrix is
$A_c(X)=(I+GX)^{-1}A$.

The associated homogeneous symplectic pencil is

The pair $(A,C)$ is **discretely detectable** if some $L\in F^{n\times p}$ makes $A-LC$ Schur stable. These are exact existential properties of the given finite matrices. A residual size or an approximate spectral estimate does not itself establish any of them.

Let $A\in F^{n\times n}$, $B\in F^{n\times m}$, $C\in F^{p\times n}$, $R=R^*\succ0$, $Q=C^*C$, and $G=BR^{-1}B^*$. Assume $(A,B)$ is continuously stabilizable and $(A,C)$ is continuously detectable, using [[def-lqr-stabilizability-and-detectability]]. Then the CARE of [[def-standard-continuous-and-discrete-riccati-equations]] has exactly one Hermitian positive-semidefinite solution $X$. $$\inf_u\int_0^\infty\bigl(x(t)^*Qx(t)+u(t)^*Ru(t)\bigr)\,dt=x_0^*Xx_0$$
is attained by $u(t)=-R^{-1}B^*Xx(t)$. Controls are locally square-integrable and states are locally absolutely continuous solutions of $\dot x=Ax+Bu$. A finite value also forces the terminal term $x(T)^*Xx(T)$ to tend to zero; this transversality is proved below.

derivations.claim: First take $A=C=R=1$ and $B=0$. Then $Q=1$; every feedback leaves $A-BK=1$, so the pair is not stabilizable. The CARE is $2X+1=0$, whose only root is $X=-1/2$; it is not positive semidefinite and its closed loop remains $1$.

Next take $A=B=R=1$ and $C=0$, so $Q=0$. The pair is stabilizable, since $K=2$ gives $A-BK=-1$, but it is not detectable because $A-LC=1$ for every $L$. The CARE is $2X-X^2=0$, with positive-semidefinite roots $X=0$ and $X=2$; the first has unstable closed loop $1$ and the second stable closed loop $-1$. Since $Q=0$, zero control has zero cost for every initial state, so the value is zero rather than the stabilizing root $X=2$. Let $\widehat X=\widehat X^*$ be a CARE candidate, $\widehat A_c=A-G\widehat X$, and

Inputs are CARE data with $Q=C^*C\succeq0$, $R\succ0$, a supplied stabilizing gain $K_0$, a finite outer budget $N$, and either exact or safeguarded-inexact solve mode. At iteration $j$, put $A_j=A-BK_j$.

In exact mode, use [[alg-bartels-stewart-sylvester-equation]] to solve
$$A_j^*X_j+X_jA_j=-(Q+K_j^*RK_j).$$
If it does not return success, stop with its status. Otherwise set $K_{j+1}=R^{-1}B^*X_j$ and continue, stopping after at most $N$ updates.

In safeguarded-inexact mode, take a proposed Hermitian approximate Lyapunov solution $\widetilde P_j$, define $\widetilde K_j=R^{-1}B^*\widetilde P_j$, and inspect the finite line-search list $\theta_\ell=2^{-\ell}$, $0\le\ell\le L$. For each trial $K_\ell=K_j+\theta_\ell(\widetilde K_j-K_j)$, let $A_\ell=A-BK_\ell$ and obtain outward-verified data: $W_\ell\succ0$, $\mu_\ell>0$ with
$$A_\ell^*W_\ell+W_\ell A_\ell\preceq-\mu_\ell I,$$
an inverse bound $\kappa_\ell\ge\|\mathcal L_{A_\ell}^{-1}\|_{F\to F}$, a residual bound $r_\ell$ for
$$\mathcal L_{A_\ell}(\widetilde P_j)+Q+K_\ell^*RK_\ell,$$
and an outward upper bound $\eta_\ell\ge\lambda_{\max}(\widetilde P_j-X_j)$. Accept the first trial satisfying $\eta_\ell+\kappa_\ell r_\ell\le0$. If none passes, return safeguard-inconclusive without changing $K_j$. The verifier uses the residual-certificate convention of [[def-verified-linear-residual-certificate-data]] and the finite-DAG enclosure guarantee of [[thm-outward-rounded-operations-are-isotone-and-dag-sound]].

After at most $N$ outer updates return the accepted gain sequence, solve residuals, cost-matrix data, and terminal status. An arbitrary approximate Lyapunov solve is never accepted without the separate stability and descent checks above.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]).

### Finite sums of vectors

By axiom (V1) the triple $(V, +, 0_V)$ is an abelian group ([[def-group]]), hence
in particular a commutative monoid ([[def-semigroup-and-monoid]]). So the finite
products of [[def-monoid-finite-product]] are available in it, and we write them
**additively**: for $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and a finite list $u : n \to V$, that is a
function on the von Neumann natural $n = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$
([[def-natural-numbers]], [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]),

$$\sum_{i<n} u_i \;:=\; \prod_{i<n} u_i \quad \text{computed in } (V,+,0_V),$$

so that $\sum_{i<0} u_i = 0_V$ and $\sum_{i<\sigma(n)} u_i = \bigl(\sum_{i<n} u_i\bigr) + u_n$,
and the value depends only on $u_0, \dots, u_{n-1}$.

### Linear combinations

A **linear combination in $V$** is a vector of the form

$$\sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i$$

where $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\lambda : n \to F$ is a finite list of scalars and
$v : n \to V$ is a finite list of vectors; the sum is the finite sum just
described, of the list $i \mapsto \lambda_i v_i$. For $S \subseteq V$, a vector
$w \in V$ is a **linear combination of elements of $S$** when there are
$n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\lambda : n \to F$ and $v : n \to S$ with
$w = \sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i$.

**The empty case is a real case.** $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$
([[def-natural-numbers]]), and at $n = 0$ the sum is the empty sum, which is
$0_V$. So $0_V$ is a linear combination of elements of every subset of $V$,
including $S = \varnothing$. The lists are indexed from $0$, so a linear
combination of length $n$ is $\lambda_0 v_0 + \dots + \lambda_{n-1}v_{n-1}$; no
statement here is restricted to $n \ge 1$.

### The span

Let $S \subseteq V$. The set of linear subspaces of $V$ containing $S$ is
nonempty, since $V$ itself is one, so its intersection is a linear subspace of
$V$ by [[lem-intersection-of-linear-subspaces]]. That intersection is the **span
of $S$**,

$$\operatorname{span}(S) \;:=\; \bigcap \{\, W \;:\; W \text{ is a linear subspace of } V \text{ and } S \subseteq W \,\} .$$

It contains $S$, being an intersection of sets each of which contains $S$, and it
is contained in every linear subspace of $V$ that contains $S$. So it is the
**smallest** linear subspace of $V$ containing $S$, and those two properties
determine it uniquely: if $W$ and $W'$ both contain $S$ and are each contained in
every linear subspace containing $S$, then each is contained in the other. This
is what licenses the definite article.

A subset $S \subseteq V$ **spans** $V$, or is a **spanning set** of $V$, when
$\operatorname{span}(S) = V$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map of vector spaces over $F$, with $V$
finite-dimensional. Then

$$\dim_F V=\operatorname{nullity}T+\operatorname{rank}T.$$

Equivalently,

$$\dim_F V=\dim_F(\ker T)+\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$

For every finite matrix over a field,
$$\operatorname{rrank}(A)=\operatorname{crank}(A).$$
Both dimensions equal the number of pivots in any echelon form of $A$.

Let $A\in M_r(F)$ and $D\in M_s(F)$. For either block-triangular matrix

$$M=\begin{pmatrix}A&C\\0&D\end{pmatrix}\quad\text{or}\quad M=\begin{pmatrix}A&0\\C&D\end{pmatrix},$$

one has $\chi_M(x)=\chi_A(x)\chi_D(x)$, including $r=0$ or $s=0$.

For an endomorphism $T$ of a finite-dimensional $F$-vector space,

$$\sigma_F(T)=\{\lambda\in F:\chi_T(\lambda)=0\}.$$

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be linear. A scalar $\lambda\in F$ is an **eigenvalue** of $T$ when there is a nonzero vector $v\in V$ such that

$$T(v)=\lambda v.$$

Such a vector is an **eigenvector belonging to $\lambda$**. The **eigenspace** belonging to $\lambda$ is

$$E_\lambda(T):=\ker(T-\lambda I_V)=\{v\in V:T(v)=\lambda v\}.$$

Thus $E_\lambda(T)$ is a linear subspace and always contains $0_V$, while $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue exactly when $E_\lambda(T)\ne\{0_V\}$. The **spectrum of $T$ over $F$** is

$$\sigma_F(T):=\{\lambda\in F:\lambda\text{ is an eigenvalue of }T\}.$$

In particular, the unique endomorphism of the zero space has empty spectrum.

derivations.claim: For each integer $k\ge0$, put $\mathcal R_k=\operatorname{span}\{A^jBe_\ell:0\le j<k,\ 1\le\ell\le m\}$. Then $\mathcal R_{k+1}=\mathcal R_k+A\mathcal R_k+\operatorname{im}B$. If $\mathcal R_{k+1}=\mathcal R_k$, then $\operatorname{im}B\subseteq\mathcal R_k$ and $A\mathcal R_k\subseteq\mathcal R_k$, so every later space equals $\mathcal R_k$. Otherwise each inclusion is strict; if no equality occurs before $\mathcal R_n$, its dimension has increased at least $n$ times from zero, hence $\mathcal R_n=F^n$. Therefore $\mathcal R=\mathcal R_n$ is the smallest $A$-invariant subspace containing $\operatorname{im}B$.

Let $(E,H)$ be reachable on $F^d$. If $[\lambda I-E\ \ H]$ had rank less than $d$ over $\mathbb C$, row-rank equality and rank-nullity applied to its adjoint would give a nonzero $y\in\mathbb C^d$ with $y^*(\lambda I-E)=0$ and $y^*H=0$. Induction then gives $y^*E^jH=\lambda^j y^*H=0$ for every $j<d$, contradicting reachability; for real data the real reachable columns complexify to span $\mathbb C^d$. Thus the horizontal rank is $d$ for every complex $\lambda$.

Scan the finite columns of $B,AB,\ldots,A^{n-1}B$, retaining a column exactly when it is outside the span of those retained; then scan the standard coordinate vectors until the retained list is a basis of $F^n$. This gives a basis matrix $P$ whose first $r$ columns span $\mathcal R$. Invariance and $\operatorname{im}B\subseteq\mathcal R$ give $P^{-1}AP=\begin{bmatrix}A_r&D\\0&A_u\end{bmatrix}$ and $P^{-1}B=\begin{bmatrix}B_r\\0\end{bmatrix}$; the first $r$ coordinates of the columns $A^jB$ are $A_r^jB_r$ and span $F^r$. Applying the stabilization argument of step 1.1 in dimension $r$ shows that the first $r$ powers already span $F^r$, so $(A_r,B_r)$ is reachable, including $r=0$. For real data, complexifying the real span gives the complex span because each complex coefficient splits into real and imaginary parts. No arbitrary basis choice is used.

For any gain $J$, a subspace $W$ contains $\operatorname{im}H$ and is $E$-invariant exactly when it contains $\operatorname{im}H$ and is $(E-HJ)$-invariant: $HJW\subseteq\operatorname{im}H\subseteq W$, and the converse follows from $E=(E-HJ)+HJ$. By step 1.1 the smallest invariant subspace containing $\operatorname{im}H$, hence reachability, is feedback-invariant.

In the block coordinates of step 2.1, $[\lambda I-A\ \ B]$ has block form $\begin{bmatrix}\lambda I-A_r&-D&B_r\\0&\lambda I-A_u&0\end{bmatrix}$. A left annihilator $(a,b)$ must satisfy $a[\lambda I-A_r\ \ B_r]=0$, so step 1.2 forces $a=0$; a nonzero remaining annihilator exists exactly when $\det(\lambda I-A_u^{\mathbb C})=0$, which by [F5] is exactly $\lambda\in\sigma_{\mathbb C}(A_u^{\mathbb C})$. Invertible coordinate changes preserve rank, proving the claimed equivalence in the original coordinates.

Prove pole placement by induction on $d$. For $d=0$ the empty gain gives determinant $1$. For $d>0$, reachability implies $\operatorname{rank}H>0$. Fix $\mu_1\in F$. By step 1.2, $[E-\mu_1I\ \ -H]$ has full row rank over $\mathbb C$; for real data a nonzero full-size minor has real nonzero determinant, so it also has full row rank over $F$. Its kernel has dimension $m$ by [F2], whereas kernel vectors with first component zero have dimension $m-\operatorname{rank}H<m$. Choose a kernel vector $(v,u)$ with $v\ne0$; it satisfies $(E-\mu_1I)v=Hu$. Choose $v_i\ne0$ and define $J_0x=u x_i/v_i$, so $(E-HJ_0)v=\mu_1v$.

Let $\pi:F^d\to F^d/Fv$ be the quotient map, $\bar E_0\pi=\pi(E-HJ_0)$, and $\bar H=\pi H$. The quotient pair is reachable because the spanning columns of $(E-HJ_0,H)$ project onto the quotient by step 2.2; the stabilization argument of step 1.1 in dimension $d-1$ shows that its first $d-1$ powers suffice. To obtain quotient coordinates over $F$, begin with $v$ and append standard coordinate vectors whenever they increase its span; the resulting finite basis has $d-1$ remaining vectors whose cosets form a basis of $F^d/Fv$. Thus the induction applies over the original field, also when $d=1$ and the quotient is zero. By induction a quotient gain $\bar J$ places $\mu_2,\ldots,\mu_d$; lift it as $J_1=\bar J\pi$ and set $J=J_0+J_1$. Since $J_1v=0$, the closed loop retains eigenvalue $\mu_1$ on $Fv$ and induces the assigned quotient characteristic polynomial. The block-triangular characteristic identity [F4] gives $\det(zI-E+HJ)=\prod_{j=1}^d(z-\mu_j)$, including repeated poles and poles already in $\sigma(E)$; no inverse of $E$ or $E-\mu I$ is used.

Let $F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, $n,m,p\ge1$, $A\in F^{n\times n}$, $B\in F^{n\times m}$, and $C\in F^{p\times n}$. A matrix is **Hurwitz** when every complex eigenvalue has strictly negative real part, as in [[def-hurwitz-matrix-and-continuous-lyapunov-equation]]. It is **Schur stable** when every complex eigenvalue has modulus strictly less than one.

The pair $(A,B)$ is **continuously stabilizable** if some $K\in F^{m\times n}$ makes $A-BK$ Hurwitz. The pair $(A,C)$ is **continuously detectable** if some $L\in F^{n\times p}$ makes $A-LC$ Hurwitz.

The pair $(A,B)$ is **discretely stabilizable** if some $K\in F^{m\times n}$ makes $A-BK$ Schur stable. The pair $(A,C)$ is **discretely detectable** if some $L\in F^{n\times p}$ makes $A-LC$ Schur stable. These are exact existential properties of the given finite matrices. A residual size or an approximate spectral estimate does not itself establish any of them.

For $A\in F^{n\times n}$, $B\in F^{n\times m}$, and $C\in F^{p\times n}$ with $F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, the following necessary conditions hold.

If $(A,B)$ is continuously stabilizable, then $\operatorname{rank}[\lambda I-A\;B]=n$ for every $\lambda\in\mathbb C$ with $\operatorname{Re}\lambda\ge0$. If it is discretely stabilizable, the same rank is $n$ for every $|\lambda|\ge1$.

If $(A,C)$ is continuously detectable, then $\operatorname{rank}\begin{bmatrix}\lambda I-A\\C\end{bmatrix}=n$ for every $\operatorname{Re}\lambda\ge0$. If it is discretely detectable, the same rank is $n$ for every $|\lambda|\ge1$.

This proves the necessary half of the PBH tests. The converse pole-placement implication is not asserted here.

Let $F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let $n,m\ge0$, and let $A\in F^{n\times n}$ and $B\in F^{n\times m}$. The real case is viewed over $\mathbb C$ when a complex spectral parameter or rank is used. Define
$$\mathcal R=\operatorname{span}_F\{A^jBe_\ell:0\le j<n,\ 1\le\ell\le m\},\qquad r=\dim_F\mathcal R,$$
where a span of an empty family is $\{0\}$. Then there is an invertible $P\in F^{n\times n}$ such that
$$P^{-1}AP=\begin{bmatrix}A_r&D\\0&A_u\end{bmatrix},\qquad P^{-1}B=\begin{bmatrix}B_r\\0\end{bmatrix}.$$
The pair $(A_r,B_r)$ is reachable on $F^r$ in the displayed algebraic sense, and empty blocks are permitted. For every $\lambda\in\mathbb C$,
$$\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb C}[\lambda I-A\ \ B]=n\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \lambda\notin\sigma_{\mathbb C}(A_u^{\mathbb C}),$$
where $A_u^{\mathbb C}$ is the complexification of $A_u$ when $F=\mathbb R$ and is $A_u$ itself when $F=\mathbb C$.

If $r=n$, then for every prescribed list $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_n\in F$ there is a gain $K\in F^{m\times n}$ satisfying
$$\det(zI-A+BK)=\prod_{j=1}^n(z-\mu_j).$$
Thus a real reachable pair can be assigned any real pole list, including repetitions, and a complex reachable pair any complex list. The pole-placement claim does not assert arbitrary nonreal conjugate-pair placement for a real pair.

Let $A\in M_r(F)$ and $D\in M_s(F)$. For either block-triangular matrix

$$M=\begin{pmatrix}A&C\\0&D\end{pmatrix}\quad\text{or}\quad M=\begin{pmatrix}A&0\\C&D\end{pmatrix},$$

one has $\chi_M(x)=\chi_A(x)\chi_D(x)$, including $r=0$ or $s=0$.

For every finite matrix over a field,
$$\operatorname{rrank}(A)=\operatorname{crank}(A).$$
Both dimensions equal the number of pivots in any echelon form of $A$.

derivations.claim: Necessity in all four assertions is exactly [F2]. This proves the forward implications from stabilizability or detectability to the stated rank tests, including every point on each closed boundary.

Fix either forbidden closed region $\Omega=\{\lambda:\operatorname{Re}\lambda\ge0\}$ or $\Omega=\{\lambda:|\lambda|\ge1\}$. Suppose the horizontal rank test holds for all $\lambda\in\Omega$, and apply [F3] to $(A,B)$ over the original field $F$. The uncontrollable block $A_u$ has no eigenvalue in $\Omega$, so its eigenvalues lie in the open left half-plane or open unit disk, respectively. Assign the reachable block repeated pole $-1$ or $0$ by [F3], obtaining $K_r$. With its decomposition matrix $P$, set $K=[K_r\ 0]P^{-1}$; if $r=0$ take $K=0$, and if $r=n$ omit the empty trailing block. Then $P^{-1}(A-BK)P=\begin{bmatrix}A_r-B_rK_r&D\\0&A_u\end{bmatrix}$. By [F4] its eigenvalues are the assigned stable poles and those of $A_u$, with multiplicity; hence $A-BK$ is Hurwitz or Schur stable, and $K\in F^{m\times n}$.

For every $\lambda\in\mathbb C$, $\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb C}[\bar\lambda I-A^*\ \ C^*]=\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb C}\begin{bmatrix}\lambda I-A\\C\end{bmatrix}$ because these matrices are adjoints and [F5] applies. Each forbidden region is invariant under conjugation, so its vertical test for $(A,C)$ is the horizontal test for $(A^*,C^*)$. Step 1.2 supplies $J\in F^{p\times n}$ with $A^*-C^*J$ Hurwitz or Schur stable. Its adjoint $A-J^*C$ has conjugate eigenvalues with the same real parts and moduli, so $L=J^*\in F^{n\times p}$ is the required injection. This proves both detectability converses, including their boundary cases.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $n\ge0$ and $A\in\mathbb F^{n\times n}$, and let $Q^*$ denote transpose over $\mathbb R$ and conjugate transpose over $\mathbb C$. A **complex Schur pair** for $A$ is a pair $(Q,T)$ with $Q^*Q=I$ and $A=QTQ^*$, where $T$ is upper triangular.

For real $A$, a **real Schur pair** is a pair $(Q,T)$ with $Q^TQ=I$ and $A=QTQ^T$, where $T$ is block upper triangular and every diagonal block is either a real $1\times1$ block or a real $2\times2$ block with negative characteristic-polynomial discriminant. Such a $2\times2$ block has one nonreal conjugate eigenvalue pair. The definition does not assert that a finite shift strategy reaches such a pair.

For $B=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb R^{2\times2}$, its characteristic-polynomial discriminant means the exact real number $\Delta(B)=(a+d)^2-4(ad-bc)$. “Negative discriminant” means the exact comparison $\Delta(B)<0$.

Let $(A,B)$ be a regular pencil of order $n$. A **complex generalized Schur
form** is a factorisation
$$Q^*AZ=S,\qquad Q^*BZ=T,$$
where $Q,Z\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ are unitary in the sense of
[[def-linear-isometry-and-orthogonal-or-unitary-operator]], and $S,T$ are
upper triangular as in
[[def-triangular-and-diagonal-matrices-over-a-commutative-ring]]. For its
$i$th one-by-one diagonal block, $[s_{ii}:t_{ii}]$ is the
**diagonal homogeneous pair**.

For real $A,B$, a **real generalized Schur form** has
$$Q^TAZ=S,\qquad Q^TBZ=T,$$
where $Q,Z$ are orthogonal, $S$ is block upper triangular with diagonal blocks
of size one or two, and $T$ is upper triangular. Each one-by-one diagonal
block has a nonzero real homogeneous pair. For a two-by-two diagonal block
$(S_{kk},T_{kk})$, the **diagonal homogeneous roots** are the zeros of
$\det(\beta S_{kk}-\alpha T_{kk})$ in $[\alpha:\beta]$; such a block has a
nonreal conjugate pair of finite roots. A singular pencil is outside this
definition.

Let $n\ge1$, let $\mathcal A$ be a nonempty set of matrices in $\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, and let $\mathcal b$ be a nonempty subset of $\mathbb C^n$. A **uniform residual certificate** consists of a point matrix $R\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, a point vector $\widehat x\in\mathbb C^n$, and numbers $q,r\ge0$ such that
$$
\|I-RA\|_2\le q,\qquad \|R(b-A\widehat x)\|_2\le r
$$
for every $A\in\mathcal A$ and $b\in\mathcal b$. Here $\|\cdot\|_2$ is the operator norm induced by the Euclidean vector norm, as in [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]]. The certificate is **usable** when $q<1$; in that case its reported error radius is $r/(1-q)$. The point-data case is $\mathcal A=\{A\}$ and $\mathcal b=\{b\}$.

This definition specifies mathematical upper bounds; it does not specify how a computation establishes them.

If $(R,\widehat x,q,r)$ is usable uniform residual certificate data for nonempty $\mathcal A\subseteq\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ and $\mathcal b\subseteq\mathbb C^n$, then for every $A\in\mathcal A$ and $b\in\mathcal b$, the equation $Ax=b$ has a unique solution $x_A(b)$ and
$$
\|x_A(b)-\widehat x\|_2\le\frac{r}{1-q}.
$$

For real intervals, complex rectangles or complex balls on which an operation
is defined, enlarging either input enclosure cannot shrink the computed
enclosure: for binary $\circ\in\{+,-,\times,\div\}$, if $X\subseteq X'$ and
$Y\subseteq Y'$, then the computed set enclosure of $X\circ Y$ is contained
in that of $X'\circ Y'$ whenever both are finite results and their domain
restrictions are preserved. The square-root enclosure is inclusion-isotone on
nonnegative intervals. Each finite ball operation in
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]] contains the exact ball
image. A `split-domain`, `entire`, `domain-error`, `overflow`, or
`inconclusive` status makes no finite claim. For a finite expression DAG
whose operation nodes all return finite enclosures, every exact node value
from every admissible input assignment belongs to its computed node
enclosure; in particular, the root enclosure contains the exact range. If any
node returns a non-finite status, no finite DAG enclosure is asserted.

Let $(v_0,\ldots,v_{r-1})$ be a finite linearly independent list in a real or complex inner product space. There is an orthonormal list $(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$ such that, for every $k\le r$,

$$\operatorname{span}(e_0,\ldots,e_{k-1})=\operatorname{span}(v_0,\ldots,v_{k-1}).$$

It is obtained recursively from

$$u_k=v_k-\sum_{j<k}\langle v_k,e_j\rangle e_j,\qquad e_k=\frac{u_k}{\lVert u_k\rVert}.$$

For $r=0$, both lists are empty.

Let $E\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, $n\ge1$, and let $0\le q<1$ satisfy $\|E\|_2\le q$. Then $I-E$ is invertible and
$$
\|(I-E)^{-1}\|_2\le \frac1{1-q}.
$$

For compatible linear maps between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces,

$$\lVert ST\rVert\le \lVert S\rVert\,\lVert T\rVert.$$

For every such linear map $T$,

$$\lVert T^*T\rVert=\lVert T\rVert^2.$$

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map of vector spaces over $F$, with $V$
finite-dimensional. Then

$$\dim_F V=\operatorname{nullity}T+\operatorname{rank}T.$$

Equivalently,

$$\dim_F V=\dim_F(\ker T)+\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$

routine_steps.claim: The validation scan and each selector test examine finitely many matrix entries or declared blocks. The listed Schur forms and homogeneous block conventions are exactly [F1] and [F2]; every sign decision either has an exact result or a finite outward enclosure by [F5]. Invalid structure, boundary equality, an unresolved enclosure, or a dimension mismatch takes its declared return branch before a swap is committed.

At each local attempt $p,q\le2$, so the coefficient matrix has order at most eight and the pivot search is finite. Complete pivoting uses invertible row and column permutations; each elimination subtracts a pivot-row multiple and is reversed by adding it back. Exact back-substitution therefore solves the recorded system or detects an exact zero remaining block. If $\|I-YH\|_2\le\theta<1$, [F7] makes $YH$ invertible; $(YH)^{-1}Y$ is a left inverse of square $H$, so [F9] makes $H$ invertible and [F8] gives $\|H^{-1}\|_2\le\|Y\|_2/(1-\theta)$. The routine still verifies $Hx=h$ exactly. An unavailable solve, comparison, or bound takes its explicit failure status.

The last $q$ rows of each graph matrix $[R;I_q]$ and $[L;I_q]$ form $I_q$, so both have independent columns. By [F6], Gram–Schmidt gives orthonormal graph columns with the same span. If the current span is proper, some standard coordinate vector lies outside it because those vectors span $F^{p+q}$; the finite scan therefore completes a basis.

All remaining loops are finite scans of blocks, rows, columns, pivots, or the bounded standard basis. Every arithmetic or evaluation request consumes one unit of $W$ before execution, and every local attempt consumes one unit of $K$ before construction. Each failure returns without committing provisional data. Thus the procedure returns a declared status after finitely many operations or reaches ordered after finitely many committed exchanges; no unresolved comparison is retried indefinitely.
