Inputs are an order $d\ge0$ real or complex Schur matrix $T$, or a regular real or complex generalized Schur pair $(S,T)$, with the declared diagonal block partition. Complex Schur and QZ forms have scalar blocks; real Schur forms have scalar blocks or real $2\times2$ blocks; real generalized Schur forms have real $1\times1$ or $2\times2$ blocks. Each generalized diagonal block pair must be regular. Optional accumulated factors are exact unitary/orthogonal products; if omitted they are identity. Other inputs are a CARE selector (strict left half-plane) or DARE selector (strict unit disk), a required integer selected dimension $0\le r\le d$, nonnegative integer budgets $K$ and $W$, a positive local separation threshold $\eta$, and either an exact arithmetic controller or a bounded outward evaluator.

Use the CARE selector with an ordinary Schur form and the DARE selector with a generalized Schur form; an unmatched form-selector combination returns invalid-form.

The entries of the input arrays are treated as their exact represented real or complex values. All local transformed arrays and accumulated factors are retained exactly as finite products; a rounded dense copy is only a separately evaluated diagnostic. Before each scalar primitive or outward evaluation, return work-budget-exhausted if no units of $W$ remain; otherwise consume one unit before requesting the operation. Charge validation, label and inversion-count scans, local construction, and the final ordering scan to this same budget. For rational or dyadic arrays, the exact core uses rational arithmetic and positive square roots, with exact real-algebraic sign comparisons where needed. Exact decisions on arbitrary real inputs are an exact-real arithmetic model, not a bit-computability claim. The bounded-evaluator branch returns arithmetic-inconclusive whenever a needed zero, sign, division, or normalization remains unresolved.

1. Validate dimensions, the declared block pattern, and regularity of each generalized diagonal pair in one finite scan. For ordinary scalar blocks over either field classify $t_{ii}$ by $\operatorname{Re}t_{ii}<0$ or $>0$ for CARE; for real $2\times2$ blocks first verify negative discriminant and then classify by trace less than or greater than zero. For generalized scalar blocks over either field $[s_{ii}:t_{ii}]$, verify the pair is nonzero and classify by $|s_{ii}|<|t_{ii}|$ or $|s_{ii}|>|t_{ii}|$ for DARE; thus $t_{ii}=0$, $s_{ii}\ne0$ is complementary and represents infinity without division. For a real generalized $2\times2$ block, verify $\det(T_b)\ne0$ and that $\det(S_b-\lambda T_b)$ has negative discriminant; its conjugate roots have common squared modulus $\det(S_b)/\det(T_b)$, so classify by strict comparison of this ratio with one, cross-multiplying with the certified sign of $\det(T_b)$. Exact equality with the selected boundary returns boundary-spectrum. A bounded enclosure touching the boundary returns separation-inconclusive. Require that the selected block sizes sum to $r$, or return dimension-mismatch. Invalid patterns or singular local homogeneous pairs return invalid-form. Compute the initial inversion count once by scanning all ordered block pairs after classification.

2. Give every whole block its selected or complementary label. Locate the leftmost adjacent complementary-selected inversion. If none exists, return ordered with the current exact arrays and accumulated factors. If an inversion exists but $K$ swap attempts have already been made, return swap-budget-exhausted. Otherwise consume one attempt before starting its local construction. Never split a real conjugate pair.

3. Let $p,q\in\{1,2\}$ be the two adjacent block sizes (over $\mathbb C$, $p=q=1$), with local blocks
$$T_{JJ}=\begin{bmatrix}A&C\\0&B\end{bmatrix}$$
for ordinary Schur form, or
$$S_{JJ}=\begin{bmatrix}A&C\\0&B\end{bmatrix},\qquad T_{JJ}=\begin{bmatrix}D&F\\0&E\end{bmatrix}$$
for QZ form. With column-vectorization, form the local coefficient system
$$H=I_q\otimes A-B^T\otimes I_p,\qquad h=-\operatorname{vec}(C)$$
for ordinary Schur, with unknown $\operatorname{vec}(R)$, and
$$H=\begin{bmatrix}I_q\otimes A&-B^T\otimes I_p\\I_q\otimes D&-E^T\otimes I_p\end{bmatrix},\qquad h=-\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{vec}(C)\\\operatorname{vec}(F)\end{bmatrix}$$
for QZ, with unknown $[\operatorname{vec}(R);\operatorname{vec}(L)]$. The transpose in $B^T$ and $E^T$ is intentional, also over $\mathbb C$. Solve $Hx=h$ and $HY=I$ by finite Gaussian elimination with complete pivoting: at each stage scan the finite remaining submatrix, choose an entry of largest certified modulus with lexicographic ties, swap rows and columns, eliminate, and back-substitute while undoing column permutations. An exact all-zero remaining submatrix returns swap-singular. An unresolved pivot or range failure returns separation-inconclusive or range-failure. Verify $Hx=h$ and $HY=I$ exactly, or verify a usable approximate-inverse certificate $\|I-YH\|_2\le\theta<1$ and still solve $Hx=h$ exactly. In the latter case it gives $\|H^{-1}\|_2\le\|Y\|_2/(1-\theta)$. In the exact-inverse branch take $\beta=\|Y\|_F$ in exact arithmetic, or an outward upper bound for that norm; in the approximate-inverse branch take an outward bound for $\|Y\|_2/(1-\theta)$. Require $\eta\beta\le1$; otherwise return swap-separation-inconclusive. Record the threshold, solves, pivot decisions and certificate.

4. For ordinary Schur form set $V=[R;I_q]$. For QZ set $V=[R;I_q]$ and $W_L=[L;I_q]$. Complete the columns of $V$, and separately $W_L$, to exact orthonormal bases by Gram–Schmidt: process the graph columns first, then $e_1,\ldots,e_{p+q}$, skipping exactly zero residuals and normalizing each nonzero residual by the positive square root of its squared norm. The graph columns are independent because their last $q$ rows form $I_q$; the coordinate scan completes a basis. An unresolved zero or normalization decision in bounded mode returns arithmetic-inconclusive.

5. Let $Z_{\rm loc}$ be the ordinary orthogonal/unitary completion; for QZ let $Z_{\rm loc}$ be the right completion and $Q_{\rm loc}$ the left completion. Propose the local transform $Z_{\rm loc}^*T Z_{\rm loc}$ in the ordinary case, or $Q_{\rm loc}^*SZ_{\rm loc}$ and $Q_{\rm loc}^*TZ_{\rm loc}$ in the QZ case. Apply it to the entire affected row and column panels, including upper off-diagonal blocks. The lower-left block is set to exact zero only by the local equations solved in step 3. For a real QZ form, factor each newly formed real $2\times2$ diagonal block as $T_b=L_bR_b$ by Gram–Schmidt on its two columns, apply the embedded $L_b^*$ to the corresponding rows of both arrays, and update $Q_{\rm loc}\leftarrow Q_{\rm loc}L_b$ with the same embedded factor; such a block is nonsingular because its roots are finite and nonreal. A size-one infinite pair requires no division by its zero second coordinate. Commit the provisional panels and factor updates only after every required local operation succeeds; otherwise return the previous committed arrays with a failed-attempt diagnostic.

6. After a committed exchange, swap the two labels and sizes and return to step 2. Ordinary accumulated factors are updated by right multiplication with $Z_{\rm loc}$; generalized accumulated factors are updated as $Q\leftarrow QQ_{\rm loc}$ and $Z\leftarrow ZZ_{\rm loc}$. The first $r$ columns of the updated factor are reported as the selected basis candidate; in QZ the right factor $Z$, not the left factor $Q$, supplies the right deflating basis.

On every exit return the current partial form, exact product factors, status, selected dimension, boundary and separation predicates, initial inversion count, attempts, accepted swaps, primitive/evaluator counts, original residual certificates, local inverse-norm certificates, and any residual transport data. Other statuses are work-budget-exhausted, arithmetic-inconclusive, range-failure, invalid-form, dimension-mismatch, boundary-spectrum, separation-inconclusive, swap-singular, swap-separation-inconclusive, and swap-budget-exhausted. ordered is distinct from any Riccati acceptance status. Reordering a computed form does not assert a structured Hamiltonian or symplectic backward-error theorem.

Let $F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, $m,n\ge1$, $A\in F^{m\times m}$ and $B\in F^{n\times n}$. Spectra of real matrices are taken over $\mathbb C$. The map $\mathcal S_{A,B}$ of [[def-sylvester-operator-and-separation-number]] is invertible if and only if

$$
\sigma(A)\cap(-\sigma(B))=\varnothing.
$$

Equivalently, for every $C\in F^{m\times n}$, the equation $AX+XB=C$ has a unique solution if and only if this spectral condition holds. The same condition is equivalent to $\operatorname{sep}(A,-B)>0$.
Let $D$ be an integral domain. A nonzero polynomial $f\in D[x]$ of degree $n$ has at most $n$ distinct roots in $D$.

Let $T:V\to V$ be a linear operator on a finite-dimensional vector space over
a field $F$. Then $T$ is invertible if and only if $\det(T)\neq0$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map of vector spaces over $F$, with $V$
finite-dimensional. Then

$$\dim_F V=\operatorname{nullity}T+\operatorname{rank}T.$$

Equivalently,

$$\dim_F V=\dim_F(\ker T)+\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$

Let $(v_0,\ldots,v_{r-1})$ be a finite linearly independent list in a real or complex inner product space. There is an orthonormal list $(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$ such that, for every $k\le r$,

$$\operatorname{span}(e_0,\ldots,e_{k-1})=\operatorname{span}(v_0,\ldots,v_{k-1}).$$

It is obtained recursively from

$$u_k=v_k-\sum_{j<k}\langle v_k,e_j\rangle e_j,\qquad e_k=\frac{u_k}{\lVert u_k\rVert}.$$

For $r=0$, both lists are empty.

For $n\ge1$ and $A,B\in M_n(R)$ over a commutative ring,
$$\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B).$$

Let $n_1,n_2\ge1$, $n=n_1+n_2$, and let $A,B\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ be
block upper triangular with the same two-block partition of sizes $n_1,n_2$,
with diagonal blocks $A_{11},A_{22}$ and
$B_{11},B_{22}$. For every $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C$,
$$\det(\beta A-\alpha B) =\det(\beta A_{11}-\alpha B_{11})\det(\beta A_{22}-\alpha B_{22}).$$

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, and
let $\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$ be the positive singular values of
$A$, where $r=\operatorname{rank}A$; write $\sigma_1=0$ when $r=0$.

1. **Spectral formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_2=\sigma_1$, where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is
   the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].
2. **Frobenius formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_F=\bigl(\sigma_1^{2}+\cdots+\sigma_r^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}$.
3. **Unitary invariance.** For every unitary $U\in M_m(\mathbb F)$ and
   $V\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ (over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$: orthogonal matrices),
   $$\lVert UAV\rVert_2=\lVert A\rVert_2,\qquad \lVert UAV\rVert_F=\lVert A\rVert_F.$$
4. **Sharp rank comparison.**
   $$\lVert A\rVert_2\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_F\;\le\;\sqrt{r}\,\lVert A\rVert_2.$$
   The lower inequality is an equality exactly when $r\le 1$; the upper
   inequality is an equality exactly when $\sigma_1=\cdots=\sigma_r$, that is,
   when all nonzero singular values coincide. In particular
   $\lVert A\rVert_F\le\sqrt{\min(m,n)}\,\lVert A\rVert_2$.

Let $E\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, $n\ge1$, and let $0\le q<1$ satisfy $\|E\|_2\le q$. Then $I-E$ is invertible and
$$
\|(I-E)^{-1}\|_2\le \frac1{1-q}.
$$

For compatible linear maps between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces,

$$\lVert ST\rVert\le \lVert S\rVert\,\lVert T\rVert.$$

For every such linear map $T$,

$$\lVert T^*T\rVert=\lVert T\rVert^2.$$

derivations.claim: For an ordinary complex scalar block the diagonal entry itself classifies the root, while a real $2\times2$ block with negative discriminant has conjugate roots with real part $\operatorname{tr}(T_b)/2$. For a generalized scalar pair $[s:t]$, a finite root is $s/t$, so $|s|<|t|$ is exactly the disk predicate and $t=0$, $s\ne0$ is infinity and complementary. For a real generalized $2\times2$ pair with finite nonreal roots, the root product is $\det(S_b)/\det(T_b)=|\lambda|^2$. Thus the procedure labels whole blocks exactly and detects equality at the selector boundary.

For ordinary adjacent diagonal blocks $A,B$, column-wise expansion gives $\operatorname{vec}(AR-RB)=(I_q\otimes A-B^T\otimes I_p)\operatorname{vec}R$. The selected and complementary spectra are disjoint, so [F2] applied to $X\mapsto AX+X(-B)$ makes this square coefficient operator invertible, giving a unique local solve.

For generalized adjacent pairs $(A,D)$ and $(B,E)$, their homogeneous root sets are disjoint and both pairs are regular. The polynomials $\det(A-\zeta D)$ and $\det(B-\zeta E)$ are nonzero of degrees at most $p,q$; among $p+q+1$ distinct real integers, [F3] gives a $\zeta$ for which $A_0=A-\zeta D$ and $B_0=B-\zeta E$ have nonzero determinants, hence are invertible by [F4]. Each homogeneous root $[\alpha:\beta]$ maps injectively to $\mu=\beta/(\alpha-\zeta\beta)$, an eigenvalue of $DA_0^{-1}$ because $D-\mu A_0=-(\beta A-\alpha D)/(\alpha-\zeta\beta)$; this also maps infinity to zero, and maps the second pair to $EB_0^{-1}$, so the ordinary spectra remain disjoint. If $AR-LB=0$ and $DR-LE=0$, then $A_0R=LB_0$, hence $R=A_0^{-1}LB_0$ and $DA_0^{-1}L=LEB_0^{-1}$; [F2] forces $L=0$, then $R=0$. The square generalized Sylvester system has zero kernel, so [F5] makes it invertible; for real blocks its real coefficient matrix has the same nonzero determinant as its complexification.

For ordinary input, $Q_0^*AQ_0=T_0+R_0$ and $Q_{\rm new}=Q_0V$ imply $Q_{\rm new}^*AQ_{\rm new}=V^*T_0V+V^*R_0V$. For QZ, substituting $Q_{\rm new}=Q_0U$ and $Z_{\rm new}=Z_0V$ into the two input relations gives residuals $U^*R_AV$ and $U^*R_BV$; [F9] preserves their Frobenius norms. These unstructured residual relations assert no structured pencil perturbation.

Each exact Gaussian-elimination pivot is nonzero; row and column permutations and row eliminations preserve the solution set. A zero remaining block before all pivots would contradict the invertibility in steps 1.2–1.3. Back-substitution gives the unique exact solution and applying the same operations to the coordinate vectors gives the inverse. In the approximate branch, $\|I-YH\|_2\le\theta<1$ and [F10] make $YH$ invertible; finite-dimensional square rank and [F11] give $\|H^{-1}\|_2=\|(YH)^{-1}Y\|_2\le\|Y\|_2/(1-\theta)$. Thus each committed swap has an exact solve and valid recorded inverse bound.

Every complementary-selected inversion can be removed by swapping an adjacent complementary-selected pair, which decreases the inversion count by one and leaves all other relative block orders unchanged. Thus $I\le b(b-1)/2$ and, after $I$ successful swaps, no inversion remains. The finite scans, local systems, and exact return branches in [F1] give a finite declared status; exhausted $K$ or $W$ returns its budget status.

The columns of $[R;I_q]$ and $[L;I_q]$ are independent because their last $q$ rows form $I_q$. Applying [F6] gives orthonormal graph columns; if their span is proper, some standard coordinate vector lies outside it, so the finite scan completes each required local basis.

In the ordinary case $AR-RB=-C$ gives $\begin{bmatrix}A&C\\0&B\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}R\\I_q\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}R\\I_q\end{bmatrix}B$. Writing $[R;I_q]=Z_1R_v$ with $R_v$ invertible shows the leading transformed block is similar to $B$. The quotient map $\pi(x,y)=x-Ry$ has kernel this graph and satisfies $\pi T_{JJ}=A\pi$, so its restriction to the orthogonal complement is an isomorphism onto the quotient and the trailing block is similar to $A$. Embedded local unitary updates preserve the surrounding block triangular zeros because rows below the pair vanish in its columns and columns before the pair vanish in its rows; the solved equations make the new lower-left block zero. Similarity preserves the characteristic polynomial and negative discriminant of a real $2\times2$ block, so whole conjugate pairs remain intact.

In the generalized case the two local equations give $S_{JJ}[R;I_q]=[L;I_q]B$ and $T_{JJ}[R;I_q]=[L;I_q]E$. Writing the graph matrices as $Z_1R_v$ and $Q_1R_w$ gives a zero lower-left block and a leading pair strictly equivalent to $(B,E)$. The full homogeneous determinant changes only by nonzero factors under exact left/right transforms [F7] and factors across diagonal pairs [F8]; cancelling the nonzero leading polynomial shows that the trailing pair has exactly the old first pair's homogeneous roots with multiplicity, including infinity and regularity. A real $2\times2$ pair with a finite nonreal conjugate root pair has nonsingular $T$ block, since otherwise its determinant polynomial has degree at most one. The prescribed QR restores triangularity of this block; applying the same left factor to both QZ arrays and to $Q$ changes the homogeneous determinant only by a nonzero factor and preserves the lower-left zero. An infinite scalar pair keeps its zero second coordinate and is never divided by it. The left update changes $Q$, while the right update changes $Z$, so the selected right deflating basis comes from $Z$.

The initial structure scan costs $O(d^2)$ scalar/evaluator units. Each local solve has order at most eight, each basis completion has bounded local dimension, and each panel update touches $O(d)$ entries; therefore $k$ attempts cost $O(d^2+kd)$. On success $k=I\le b(b-1)/2\le d(d-1)/2$, giving $O(d^3)$ worst-case swap work. Evaluating $L_0$ bounded-support input factors on $r$ columns costs $O(L_0dr+Idr)$; dense residual multiplication costs its separate $O(d^3)$. These counts do not bound algebraic bit cost or evaluator implementation cost.

Under the stated sufficient conditions, including enough $W$ for every scan through the final ordered return, steps 2.2 and 4.1–4.3 show that all selected blocks move before every complementary block without splitting real pairs; the first $r$ factor columns therefore span the selected invariant subspace or right deflating subspace of the represented computed form. Step 1.4 transports only the original unstructured residual certificate. Algorithm [F1] returns explicitly on boundary, separation, arithmetic, range, form, and budget failures; none of those statuses proves nonexistence of a stabilizing Riccati solution or supplies structured backward error.

boundaries.evidence: Statement: the d=0 ordinary form has no blocks or inversions, so the sufficient success condition gives ordered without swaps.
Statement: exhausted K or W yields the corresponding explicit status; the theorem claims ordered only when K and W suffice.
Step 2.2: for one scalar block the inversion count I=0 and the selected factor columns give the whole selected space.
Steps 1.2, 4.1 and 4.2 preserve infinite homogeneous roots, regularity and real conjugate blocks.
Statement: the strict selector premise excludes boundary roots; the algorithm returns boundary-spectrum when a root lies on the selector boundary.
The algorithm’s finite scans and exact basis completion supply every choice; steps 2.1–2.2 prove the local construction.

boundaries.reason: The statement gives a sufficient success condition, not a biconditional.
The statement gives a sufficient success condition, not a biconditional.

finite_checks.name: two-block inversion count and local spectrum exchange
finite_checks.calculation: The block sequence is complementary-selected, so I=1=b(b−1)/2. The exact local graph solve has R=0, and the orthogonal permutation exchanges the two scalar spectra, giving diag(1/2,2) and the selected subspace span(e2) in original coordinates.

citations.quote:
Let $X\succeq0$ be the stabilizing DARE solution, $G=BR^{-1}B^*$, and
$$N=\begin{bmatrix}A&0\\-Q&I\end{bmatrix},\qquad M=\begin{bmatrix}I&G\\0&A^*\end{bmatrix},\qquad A_c=A-B(R+B^*XB)^{-1}B^*XA.$$
Then
$$N\begin{bmatrix}I\\X\end{bmatrix}=M\begin{bmatrix}I\\X\end{bmatrix}A_c.$$
The pencil $(N,M)$ is regular. Its homogeneous determinant has n roots strictly inside the unit disk and n roots strictly outside the closed unit disk, with infinite roots counted in the latter group. Thus it has no unit-circle roots, even if $A$ is singular, and $\operatorname{Ran}\begin{bmatrix}I\\X\end{bmatrix}$ is its stable deflating graph.

Let $(A,B)$ be a regular pencil of order $n$. A **complex generalized Schur
form** is a factorisation
$$Q^*AZ=S,\qquad Q^*BZ=T,$$
where $Q,Z\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ are unitary in the sense of
[[def-linear-isometry-and-orthogonal-or-unitary-operator]], and $S,T$ are
upper triangular as in
[[def-triangular-and-diagonal-matrices-over-a-commutative-ring]]. For its
$i$th one-by-one diagonal block, $[s_{ii}:t_{ii}]$ is the
**diagonal homogeneous pair**.

For real $A,B$, a **real generalized Schur form** has
$$Q^TAZ=S,\qquad Q^TBZ=T,$$
where $Q,Z$ are orthogonal, $S$ is block upper triangular with diagonal blocks
of size one or two, and $T$ is upper triangular. Each one-by-one diagonal
block has a nonzero real homogeneous pair. For a two-by-two diagonal block
$(S_{kk},T_{kk})$, the **diagonal homogeneous roots** are the zeros of
$\det(\beta S_{kk}-\alpha T_{kk})$ in $[\alpha:\beta]$; such a block has a
nonreal conjugate pair of finite roots. A singular pencil is outside this
definition.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$ and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$. The **Frobenius norm** of $A$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_F\;:=\;\Bigl(\,\sum_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|^{2}\Bigr)^{1/2},$$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value on $\mathbb R$
([[def-abs-value]]) for $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ and the modulus on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]) for
$\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, and the outer power is the nonnegative real square root.

**The displayed quantity is a norm.** Regard $A$ as the element of the
coordinate space $\mathbb F^{mn}$ whose $j+in$-th entry is $a_{ij}$. The
standard coordinate inner product of [[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]
satisfies $\langle A,A\rangle=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}\overline{a_{ij}}$, which equals
$\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|^{2}$ because $z\overline z=|z|^{2}$
([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]). Thus $\lVert A\rVert_F$ is
exactly the inner-product norm of [[def-inner-product-norm]] evaluated at $A$,
and the three norm axioms hold for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_F$ because they hold for
every inner-product norm. For real matrices the same sum is
$\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^{2}$, since $|x|^{2}=x^{2}$ for real $x$ by the two cases of
[[def-abs-value]].

The Frobenius norm is the Euclidean norm of the full entry list, not the
largest factor by which the matrix stretches a single vector. It can coincide
with an induced $2$-norm in one-row or one-column cases, but in general it is a
different matrix norm from the induced operator norms used on this page. Its
relation to the spectral norm, its unitary invariance and its singular-value
formula are
[[thm-spectral-and-frobenius-norms-are-unitarily-invariant-with-singular-value-formulas-and-rank-comparison]].

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, and
let $\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$ be the positive singular values of
$A$, where $r=\operatorname{rank}A$; write $\sigma_1=0$ when $r=0$.

1. **Spectral formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_2=\sigma_1$, where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is
   the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].
2. **Frobenius formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_F=\bigl(\sigma_1^{2}+\cdots+\sigma_r^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}$.
3. **Unitary invariance.** For every unitary $U\in M_m(\mathbb F)$ and
   $V\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ (over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$: orthogonal matrices),
   $$\lVert UAV\rVert_2=\lVert A\rVert_2,\qquad \lVert UAV\rVert_F=\lVert A\rVert_F.$$
4. **Sharp rank comparison.**
   $$\lVert A\rVert_2\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_F\;\le\;\sqrt{r}\,\lVert A\rVert_2.$$
   The lower inequality is an equality exactly when $r\le 1$; the upper
   inequality is an equality exactly when $\sigma_1=\cdots=\sigma_r$, that is,
   when all nonzero singular values coincide. In particular
   $\lVert A\rVert_F\le\sqrt{\min(m,n)}\,\lVert A\rVert_2$.

For compatible linear maps between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces,

$$\lVert ST\rVert\le \lVert S\rVert\,\lVert T\rVert.$$

For every such linear map $T$,

$$\lVert T^*T\rVert=\lVert T\rVert^2.$$

Let $M\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ be Schur stable and let $r$ satisfy $\rho(M)<r<1$. For the Euclidean induced operator norm there is a finite $C_r$ such that
$$\|M^k\|_2\le C_r r^k\qquad(k\ge0).$$
For a real matrix, interpret the same statement on its complexification.

Let $X$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and assume
$X$ admits an ordered basis of finite length. Then $X$ is a Banach space in the
sense of [[def-banach-space]].

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be non-negative. Then there exists a unique non-negative operator
$R:V\to V$ such that

$$R^2=T.$$

Let $n_1,n_2\ge1$, $n=n_1+n_2$, and let $A,B\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ be
block upper triangular with the same two-block partition of sizes $n_1,n_2$,
with diagonal blocks $A_{11},A_{22}$ and
$B_{11},B_{22}$. For every $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C$,
$$\det(\beta A-\alpha B) =\det(\beta A_{11}-\alpha B_{11})\det(\beta A_{22}-\alpha B_{22}).$$
Every endomorphism of a finite-dimensional vector space over an algebraically closed field has a Jordan canonical form over that field, including the endomorphism of the zero space.

Let $E\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, $n\ge1$, and let $0\le q<1$ satisfy $\|E\|_2\le q$. Then $I-E$ is invertible and
$$
\|(I-E)^{-1}\|_2\le \frac1{1-q}.
$$

For $n\ge1$ and $A,B\in M_n(R)$ over a commutative ring,
$$\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B).$$
Let $D$ be an integral domain. A nonzero polynomial $f\in D[x]$ of degree $n$ has at most $n$ distinct roots in $D$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let
$A,B\in\mathbb F^{n\times n}$. The **matrix pencil** determined by $(A,B)$ is
$A-\lambda B$. Its determinant polynomial is
$f(\lambda)=\det(A-\lambda B)$, with real coefficients viewed as complex
coefficients when $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$. The pencil is **regular** if $f$ is
not the zero polynomial; otherwise it is **singular**.

For $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C$ not both zero, put
$$p(\alpha,\beta)=\det(\beta A-\alpha B).$$
A **homogeneous generalized eigenvalue pair** is an equivalence class of such
pairs satisfying $p(\alpha,\beta)=0$, where $(\alpha,\beta)$ and
$(c\alpha,c\beta)$ represent the same pair for every $c\in\mathbb C\setminus
\{0\}$. If $\beta\ne0$, the associated finite generalized eigenvalue is
$\lambda=\alpha/\beta$; if $\beta=0$, the pair is an infinite generalized
eigenvalue. The pair $(0,0)$ is never an eigenvalue pair.
Write $\sigma(A,B)$ for the set of finite ratios $\alpha/\beta$ among these
homogeneous eigenvalue pairs.

The QZ results on this page assume a regular pencil. They make no assertion
about Kronecker structure or eigenvalues of a singular pencil.

derivations.claim: By [F1], the regular base DARE pencil has an $n+n$ stable/outside split, and the ordered representation [F2] puts the stable roots in the leading blocks and the outside roots in the trailing blocks. Write trailing diagonal pairs as $(s_i,t_i)$ and leading ones as $(p_j,q_j)$. Disjoint homogeneous roots give $p_jt_i-s_iq_j\ne0$ for every $i,j$, including $t_i=0$. In the system $S_{22}Y-ZS_{11}=C$, $T_{22}Y-ZT_{11}=D$, process rows $i=n,n-1,\ldots,1$ and within each row columns $j=1,\ldots,n$; upper triangularity makes all other terms involve already determined $Y_{kj}$ with $k>i$ or $Z_{i\ell}$ with $\ell<j$. The two unknowns $(Y_{ij},Z_{ij})$ have coefficient matrix $\begin{bmatrix}s_i&-p_j\\t_i&-q_j\end{bmatrix}$ with determinant $p_jt_i-s_iq_j\ne0$, so the lower-oriented generalized Sylvester map is bijective. Its minimum singular value [F3] is therefore $\gamma>0$, and its inverse norm is $\kappa=\gamma^{-1}$.

Define $C_Y=S_{11}+E_{11}+(S_{12}+E_{12})Y$ and $D_Y=T_{11}+F_{11}+(T_{12}+F_{12})Y$. Block multiplication gives $(S+E)[I;Y]=[I;Z]C_Y$ and $(T+F)[I;Y]=[I;Z]D_Y$ exactly when $\mathcal L(Y,Z)=(S_{22}Y-ZS_{11},T_{22}Y-ZT_{11})$ equals $(-E_{21}-E_{22}Y+ZE_{11}+Z(S_{12}+E_{12})Y,\,-F_{21}-F_{22}Y+ZF_{11}+Z(T_{12}+F_{12})Y)$. On the product radius-$r$ ball, the right side has norm at most $\delta+2\delta r+(h+\delta)r^2$: the constant pair is bounded by $\delta$, the two linear pairs by $\delta\|Y\|_F$ and $\delta\|Z\|_F$, and the quadratic pair by $(h+\delta)\|Z\|_F\|Y\|_F$. Splitting the quadratic difference into its $Y$ and $Z$ changes bounds the Lipschitz constant by $2\delta+2(h+\delta)r$. Applying $\mathcal L^{-1}$ gives a self-map and contraction under the stated inequalities; iteration from zero has geometrically summable increments, so completeness [F8] gives a limit in the closed ball, continuity gives a fixed point, and contraction gives uniqueness. For $r=2\kappa\delta$ and $\theta=\kappa\delta$, substitution gives self-map ratio $\kappa[\delta+2\delta r+(h+\delta)r^2]/r=1/2+2\theta+2\kappa h\theta+2\theta^2$ and contraction constant $2\theta+4\kappa h\theta+4\theta^2$; the displayed strict condition implies both. For $\delta=0$, the exact pair $Y=Z=0$ solves the graph equations.

Set $R_Y=\begin{bmatrix}I&0\\Y&I\end{bmatrix}$ and $L_Z=\begin{bmatrix}I&0\\-Z&I\end{bmatrix}$. They are invertible shears of determinant one, and the graph equations from step 2.1 give $L_Z(S+E)R_Y=\begin{bmatrix}C_Y&S_{12}+E_{12}\\0&A'\end{bmatrix}$ and $L_Z(T+F)R_Y=\begin{bmatrix}D_Y&T_{12}+F_{12}\\0&B'\end{bmatrix}$, where $A'=S_{22}+E_{22}-Z(S_{12}+E_{12})$ and $B'=T_{22}+F_{22}-Z(T_{12}+F_{12})$. Unitary invariance, $\|M\|_2\le\|M\|_F$ [F5], and submultiplicativity [F6] give $\|C_Y-S_{11}\|_2,\|A'-S_{22}\|_2\le a$ and $\|D_Y-T_{11}\|_2,\|B'-T_{22}\|_2\le b$. Every leading stable root is finite, so $T_{11}$ is invertible and $K_s=T_{11}^{-1}S_{11}$ is upper triangular with diagonal moduli below one. Every trailing outside root has nonzero first homogeneous coordinate, so $S_{22}$ is invertible and $K_u=S_{22}^{-1}T_{22}$ is upper triangular with diagonal moduli below one, including zero for infinity; thus both are Schur stable. By [F7], $W_j=\sum_{k\ge0}(K_j^*)^kK_j^k$ converges for $j=s,u$, is positive definite, and satisfies $W_j-K_j^*W_jK_j=I$. The two Neumann margins and [F12] make $D_Y,A'$ invertible with inverse norms at most $\|T_{11}^{-1}\|_2/(1-\|T_{11}^{-1}\|_2b)$ and $\|S_{22}^{-1}\|_2/(1-\|S_{22}^{-1}\|_2a)$. The identities $D_Y^{-1}C_Y-K_s=D_Y^{-1}[(C_Y-S_{11})-(D_Y-T_{11})K_s]$ and $A'^{-1}B'-K_u=A'^{-1}[(B'-T_{22})-(A'-S_{22})K_u]$ give exactly the stated $\epsilon_s,\epsilon_u$ bounds.

Put $P_Y=(I+Y^*Y)^{-1/2}$. Since $V=[U\ V_2]$ is unitary, $(U+V_2Y)^*(U+V_2Y)=I+Y^*Y$, so $\widehat U^*\widehat U=I$ and $U^*\widehat U=P_Y$. Therefore $(\widehat U-U)^*(\widehat U-U)=2(I-P_Y)$. The largest eigenvalue of $Y^*Y$ is $y^2$, so [F3], [F5], and [F9] give the exact norm $\|\widehat U-U\|_2=\beta(y)$. The scalar function $g(t)=t-2(1-(1+t)^{-1/2})$ has $g(0)=0$ and $g'(t)=1-(1+t)^{-3/2}\ge0$ for $t\ge0$, proving $\beta(y)\le y\le r$. Also $(I-UU^*)\widehat U=V_2YP_Y$, whose largest singular value is $y/\sqrt{1+y^2}$ by [F3] and [F5].

If $K$ is either quotient in step 3.1 and $\|H\|_2\le\epsilon$, then $W-(K+H)^*W(K+H)=I-(K^*WH+H^*WK+H^*WH)$. The subtracted Hermitian term has norm at most $\|W\|_2(2\|K\|_2\epsilon+\epsilon^2)<1$, so the left side is positive definite; an eigenvector of $K+H$ with eigenvalue $\lambda$ gives $(1-|\lambda|^2)v^*Wv>0$, hence $|\lambda|<1$. Applied to $D_Y^{-1}C_Y$ and $A'^{-1}B'$, this makes the leading perturbed roots finite and stable, and the trailing roots outside, with zero eigenvalues of $A'^{-1}B'$ representing infinity. The shears have determinant one, so [F13] preserves the homogeneous determinant under their left/right transformations; [F10] factors it across the diagonal blocks. Since $D_Y$ and $A'$ are invertible, both diagonal pencils are regular and their product is a regular pencil with the claimed $n+n$ root split. The regular base and perturbed determinant polynomials have finite root sets by [F14]; choose $\lambda_0\in\mathbb C$ outside their union. Put $\mathcal R=(N'-\lambda_0M')^{-1}M'$ for $N'=L_Z(S+E)R_Y$ and $M'=L_Z(T+F)R_Y$. Then $N'-\lambda M'=(N'-\lambda_0M')[I-(\lambda-\lambda_0)\mathcal R]$, so [F13] expresses the pencil determinant as a nonzero constant times $\det(I-(\lambda-\lambda_0)\mathcal R)$. Jordan form [F11] factors the latter into $\prod_j(1-(\lambda-\lambda_0)\mu_j)$ over the eigenvalues $\mu_j$ of $\mathcal R$, with algebraic multiplicity. Thus each finite root maps injectively to $\mu=1/(\lambda-\lambda_0)$, and the polynomial degree is the number of nonzero $\mu_j$, counted with algebraic multiplicity. Its homogeneous form is $\det(\beta N'-\alpha M')=\beta^{2n}\det(N'-(\alpha/\beta)M')$; by [F15], its multiplicity at $[1:0]$ is $2n$ minus that degree, exactly the multiplicity of the zero eigenvalue of $\mathcal R$. The matrix $\mathcal R$ is block upper triangular with diagonal blocks $(C_Y-\lambda_0D_Y)^{-1}D_Y$ and $(A'-\lambda_0B')^{-1}B'$, whose spectra are disjoint because their pencil-root groups are disjoint and the projective map is injective. For a generalized eigenvector $[x;y]$ belonging to a leading-block eigenvalue $\mu$, its trailing equation is $(\mathcal R_{22}-\mu I)^k y=0$; disjoint spectra force $y=0$. Conversely, Jordan form [F11] supplies a basis of generalized eigenvectors of the leading $n\times n$ block, which embed as $[x;0]$ and span exactly the full leading-root generalized eigenspace. Undoing the graph shears and unitary factors identifies this right subspace with $V[I;Y]$ and its matching left deflating graph with $Q[I;Z]$.

Write $\Delta U=\widehat U-U$. Under the strict chart margin, $\widehat U_1=U_1(I+U_1^{-1}\Delta U_1)$ and $\|U_1^{-1}\Delta U_1\|_2\le\|U_1^{-1}\|_2\beta(y)<1$. By [F12], $\widehat U_1$ is invertible and $\|\widehat U_1^{-1}\|_2\le(\|U_1^{-1}\|_2^{-1}-\beta(y))^{-1}$. Using $U_2=XU_1$ gives $\widehat U_2\widehat U_1^{-1}-X=(\Delta U_2-X\Delta U_1)\widehat U_1^{-1}$; [F6] yields the stated chart estimate. Since $\beta$ is increasing and $\beta(y)\le\beta(r)$, the stronger margin $\|U_1^{-1}\|_2\beta(r)<1$ gives the computable weaker bound. An independently rotated orthonormal basis of the same space is $\widehat U R_0$ for unitary $R_0$ and has the same chart because $(\widehat U_1R_0)^{-1}=R_0^{-1}\widehat U_1^{-1}$. The proof assumes no structure on $E,F$, so it gives no Riccati residual, symmetry, positivity, or post-symmetrization stability certificate.

As $\delta\to0$ with $r=2\kappa\delta$, $\theta\to0$, $a,b\to0$, and $\epsilon_s,\epsilon_u\to0$; hence the contraction, Neumann, and both Stein margins in the Statement hold for all sufficiently small $\delta$. If $U_1$ is invertible, also $\|U_1^{-1}\|_2\beta(r)<1$ for all sufficiently small $\delta$, so the computable chart margin holds. [given, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

No arbitrary Axiom of Choice is used: all constructions are finite-dimensional scans, norm-convergent series, or selections from complements of finite subsets of $\mathbb C$.
